title: Creating an LLM maintained knowledge base has saved me a lot of time and tokens during my development sessions
author: u3030
selftext:
Hey all, 

I saw this article yesterday and thought it was worth trying out ([Karpathy shares 'LLM Knowledge Base' architecture](https://venturebeat.com/data/karpathy-shares-llm-knowledge-base-architecture-that-bypasses-rag-with-an)).  I wanted to share the article and some of my results, as I think it might help some folks here who might be like me and have a series of different projects and tools they're working on.  

  
The TLDR is I created a centralized, cross-project knowledge base.  I use Claude Code, so I was able to add a custom skill that I can call while working.  Claude will document and update new information across the knowledge base for the project I am working on, and any other impacted projects (I frequently work cross project). This includes details on how each system works, key learnings, gotchas, and other relevant information. 

The reason this is helpful is, often times if I have to spin up a new session, clear context, compact. Claude spends a lot of time re-learning how these tools work.  If I build a new tool, my other sessions don't know it exists yet.  Same goes for when I make an update to one of my tools. 

All of these things take up time and tokens.  With the knowledge base intact, one single tool call can bring up the needed context for them without having to investigate sessions, files, commits, etc.  It's just in a series of linked md files and ready to go. 

For an example, I have a tool I've been working on that does a lot of work on asset generation.  It takes my concept art, runs it through Trellis or Meshy for a 3d model, decimates the model in blender, then auto rigs and animates with MIA, rigs up weapons and gear, builds sprite sheets, etc..  This is a lot, across several ComfyUI workflows, apis, mcps  and other tools being used.  

When I spun up a new project recently, it took about 80k tokens across 40 tool calls to fully get back up to speed with how the process worked.  With the knowledge base in place, it takes 1 tool call and about 3k tokens.  

This only took me an hour or so to setup, so it's definitely worth taking a look.  There are other ways to do this of course.  If you have a very large codebase, it won't work as well, but for smaller to medium size project it could be very useful.

comments.author: PenniesInTheNameOf
comments.body:
I still don’t understand.

It’s a text file? You feed it into a fresh session and now it knows what you are working with?

replies.author: u3030
replies.body: Righ, it writes and maintains a small set of .md files containing the current state of the project and related tools.  In later sessions or when calling in a new tool, the agent reads those files first, so if they’re up to date, it already knows the background, decisions, and structure without needing a bunch of extra tool calls.

comments.author: HLCYSWAP
comments.body:
why not vectorize the knowledge base? karpathy is an intelligent dude, i dont get why hes got thousands of .MDs sitting around. after a certain point the context size of the knowledge base exceeds the models input limit and you get truncated understandings or missed documents entirely because it doesnt intuit correctly what to search. he's using the model as retriever and reasoner. 

it's easy to use a LLM to do accurate embedding. his method works extremely well for small data but if youre trying to make a truly complete understanding of the universe (everything is relational) it looks like it breaks down at a phasic token limit

replies.author: u3030
replies.body: Right, I even mentioned if you have a very large codebase, this isn't going to work as well.  That's the point where you'd want to start introducing RAG.  It's really a matter of scale and what approach fits best for the job.  I think the point is that a lot of people reach for vectorization too early when there's a simpler solution.  I also believe (unverified) that a lot of the people creating here fit more into the small team/solo dev category where this approach might make more sense.

replies.author: throwaway12222018
replies.body:
Why not vectorize the knowledge base, give each dominant an ID, and have an update trigger that extracts causality, topics, and embedded IDs from the documents and stores relationships in neo4j.

Then you can ask questions like "why did i end up doing XYZ". MD alone gives you inefficient search, vectorizing gives you semantic search, adding a knowledge graph gives you relational search

replies.author: HLCYSWAP
replies.body: that's probably a much better solution. im going to look into this, i want to start a new pet project

replies.author: corysama
replies.body:
Almost related: EA shares how they vectorized their huge legacy codebase so AI can understand it better.

https://youtu.be/jFFOC3UZTTk

replies.author: throwaway12222018
replies.body:
Postgres has vector search, you just need a way to generate embeddings. Can use open ai endpoints for that. I was wondering if i should even be using markdown files anymore or if my plans, docs, memories, etc should just get added to a loosely structured pg table with all sorts of metadata, like timestamps, tags, then run vectorized search over every single document produced out of my sessions. Throw in some smart indexing and a couple of mcp tools for Claude to do CRUD on the documents, then add that as a skill or your preferred place in your workflow.

It's actually not that hard to implement tbh. There's a benefit to storing stuff in git which is my main blocker for pursuing this. Plus the table needs to be unstructured to accommodate changing types. Maybe like a title, body, and a parent_id FK to the same table. Add a recursive CTE exposed over mcp for fetching memory chains. 

But then you start wondering if you should be using a graph DB instead.

replies.author: corysama
replies.body:
Then you realize your knowledge base isn’t that huge and Obsidian is effectively a human-readable graph database. So, you just use that instead :P

https://obsidian.md/ is working for me and it’s working for Karpathy. I wouldn’t try to stuff EA’s code base into it. But, for tracking linked rules and designs for a single project, and Obsidian vault with a brief doc about its markdown extensions is very effective.

replies.author: throwaway12222018
replies.body: True. I think they actually use a graph database under the hood probably for their mind map view

comments.author: LeafyWolf
comments.body: Thanks for this.  I just had Claude build a skill that builds bespoke knowledge base skills for projects on-demand, because I didn't want to have to re-architect and prompt it every time I start a new project.

replies.author: u3030
replies.body: Nice!  Simple setup yeah?  Hope it helps you out, so far I'm really happy with it.

replies.author: LeafyWolf
replies.body: Super simple.  VERY helpful when working on multiple small projects.  Probably need a different architecture if I was working on a triple A title with a huge code base, but for a solo dev, this works great.  I'd kind of started developing something similar organically, but this architecture is much better thought out.
